title: Local Sidereal Clock
intro: Local mean sidereal time (LST) tracks Earth's rotation relative to the celestial reference frame, rather than the Sun. It helps describe which right ascension is crossing the local meridian.
structure: The display is a 24-hour angular coordinate, labelled LST. One complete cycle takes approximately 23 hours 56 minutes of ordinary time. A longitude of 15 degrees east adds one sidereal hour to Greenwich mean sidereal time.
example: At the model's J2000 reference instant, 1 January 2000 at 12:00 UTC, Greenwich reads approximately 18:41:50 LST. At longitude 15 degrees east the same model reads 19:41:50 LST. These are calculated reference values, not observations.
history: Sidereal time is an established astronomical coordinate for relating celestial objects to local meridian transit. Mean sidereal time differs from apparent sidereal time, which includes additional corrections.
model: Form JD = 2440587.5 + Unix microseconds / 86400000000. For D = JD - 2451545.0, compute Greenwich mean sidereal hours = 18.697374558 + 24.06570982441908 × D. Add east-positive longitude / 15, wrap modulo 24 and floor displayed fields. For scheduling, divide the remaining sidereal seconds by the sidereal-to-civil rate before rounding milliseconds upward.
limits: The compact J2000 model treats the Unix-based UTC coordinate as its time argument. It does not implement full IAU precession/nutation, Earth orientation or UT1 corrections. Longitude must be finite within -180 to +180 degrees; no longitude means unavailable, not Greenwich. Latitude is not used by the calculation. DUT1 and site-specific observing practice are not supplied by the provider interface.
